glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Coming down from the mountain, Jesus shows the authority of His word in action: He cleanses a leper, heals a Gentile’s servant from a distance, heals and delivers many, calls followers to costly allegiance, stills a storm, and frees two demon-possessed men.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Matthew 8 follows the Sermon on the Mount and begins the account of Jesus’ mighty works that continues through chapter 9, around Capernaum and the Sea of Galilee.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:
• Matthew 8:1–4 — Jesus Cleanses a Leper

  • Matthew 8:5–13 — The Centurion’s Faith and the Healing of His Servant

  • Matthew 8:14–17 — Healings at Peter’s House

  • Matthew 8:18–22 — The Cost of Following Jesus

  • Matthew 8:23–27 — Jesus Calms the Storm

  • Matthew 8:28–34 — Jesus Delivers Two Demon-Possessed Men

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “So the men marveled, saying, ‘Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him?’” (Matthew 8:27)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
The crowds had marveled that Jesus taught “as one having authority” (7:29). Now they see that authority at work. He reaches out and touches a leper, and the man is clean. A Roman centurion asks Him only to speak a word, and Jesus marvels at a Gentile’s faith, telling of many who will come from east and west to feast with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. At Peter’s house He heals the sick and casts out spirits, and Matthew hears Isaiah’s words: “He Himself took our infirmities and bore our sicknesses” (8:17). The Servant is already lifting the burdens of the redemption He came to bring.

In the middle of the healings Jesus makes clear what following Him costs. Then He shows who He is. A single rebuke calms the sea, and the disciples ask, “Who can this be?” On the other shore, demons recognize Him as the Son of God and beg to be sent into the swine. The men are freed, yet the townspeople plead with Jesus to leave. His presence brings rescue, and it also demands a response.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Matthew 8:1–4 — Jesus Cleanses a Leper

Jesus touches a leper and makes him clean with a word. He sends the man to show himself to the priest as Moses commanded, as a testimony.

Matthew 8:5–13 — The Centurion’s Faith and the Healing of His Servant

A centurion trusts Jesus to heal his servant simply by speaking, and Jesus praises his faith above any He has found in Israel. He warns that many from east and west will share the feast of the kingdom while sons of the kingdom are cast out.

Matthew 8:14–17 — Healings at Peter’s House

Jesus heals Peter’s mother-in-law, who rises and serves Him, and that evening He heals the sick and casts out spirits with a word. Matthew sees Isaiah 53:4 fulfilled in these healings.

Matthew 8:18–22 — The Cost of Following Jesus

A scribe offers to follow Jesus anywhere, and Jesus warns that the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head. To a disciple who wants to bury his father first, He says, “Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead” (8:22).

Matthew 8:23–27 — Jesus Calms the Storm

Jesus sleeps through a great storm on the sea until His frightened disciples wake Him. He rebukes their little faith, then rebukes the winds and sea, and there is a great calm.

Matthew 8:28–34 — Jesus Delivers Two Demon-Possessed Men

In the country of the Gergesenes, two fierce demon-possessed men meet Jesus, and the demons recognize Him as the Son of God. He sends them into a herd of swine that rushes into the sea, and the whole city begs Him to leave.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Matthew 8 shows that the King’s authority is not limited to words on a mountain. It reaches disease, distance, nature, and the powers of darkness, and it is joined to compassion. He touches the untouchable and welcomes a Gentile’s faith. These healings belong to the salvation Christ brings, so His people may pray with bold expectation, while the complete renewal of the body awaits the resurrection (Romans 8:23).

The chapter also shows that seeing Jesus’ power does not automatically produce faith. A Roman soldier trusts Him, the disciples fear in the storm, and a whole town asks Him to go away. Following Him takes priority over comfort and every other claim.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Authority of His word. Jesus heals, calms, and delivers by speaking (8:3, 8, 16, 26, 32).

Faith from unexpected places. A Gentile centurion trusts Jesus’ authority (8:10–12).

The Servant who heals. Jesus fulfills Isaiah 53:4 by healing the sick (8:17).

The cost of following. Discipleship comes before security and every competing claim (8:19–22).

Who is this? The calming of the sea and the demons’ cry reveal Jesus’ identity (8:27, 29).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Leprosy (8:2). One of the serious skin disorders that made a person ceremonially unclean and separated from the community. Jesus’ touch shows His compassion, and the cleansing and the visit to the priest open the way back to ordinary community life (8:4).

Centurion (8:5). A Roman officer over about a hundred soldiers. As a Gentile, he understood authority and trusted Jesus to command healing from a distance.

Son of Man (8:20). Jesus’ favorite name for Himself, drawn from Daniel 7:13–14. Here it joins His future dominion with His present homelessness.

Little faith (8:26). Faith present but overwhelmed by fear. Jesus rebukes the disciples, then rescues them.

Gergesenes (8:28). The people of a largely Gentile region on the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee, where the herd of swine was kept.

outline: Matthew 8:5–13 — The Centurion’s Faith and the Healing of His Servant
Matthew 8:18–22 — The Cost of Following Jesus
Matthew 8:28–34 — Jesus Delivers Two Demon-Possessed Men

focus: Matthew 8 shows the authority heard in the Sermon on the Mount at work in Jesus’ deeds as He cleanses a leper, heals a centurion’s servant by His word, and heals many sick and demon-possessed people, fulfilling Isaiah’s word about the Servant. Between these works He confronts would-be followers with the cost of following Him, stills a great storm, and casts demons out of two men in the country of the Gergesenes, whose city then begs Him to leave.

sections.title: Jesus Cleanses a Leper
sections.summary: As great multitudes follow Jesus down from the mountain, a leper worships Him and says, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean” (Matthew 8:2). Jesus touches him and he is cleansed, and Jesus tells him to tell no one but to show himself to the priest and offer the gift Moses commanded as a testimony.

sections.title: The Centurion’s Faith and the Healing of His Servant
sections.summary: A centurion in Capernaum asks Jesus to heal his paralyzed servant and says that Jesus need only speak a word, since he too knows what it is to be under authority and to give commands. Jesus marvels at his faith, declares that many will come from east and west to sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven while the sons of the kingdom are cast out, and heals the servant that same hour.

sections.title: Healings at Peter’s House
sections.summary: Jesus touches the hand of Peter’s wife’s mother, the fever leaves her, and she rises and serves them. That evening He casts out spirits with a word and heals all who are sick, fulfilling Isaiah’s word, “He Himself took our infirmities And bore our sicknesses” (Matthew 8:17).

sections.title: The Cost of Following Jesus
sections.summary: When a scribe promises to follow Jesus wherever He goes, Jesus answers that “the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head” (Matthew 8:20). When another disciple asks first to go and bury his father, Jesus replies, “Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead” (Matthew 8:22).

sections.title: Jesus Calms the Storm
sections.summary: A great tempest arises while Jesus sleeps in the boat, and His disciples wake Him, crying, “Lord, save us! We are perishing!” (Matthew 8:25). He rebukes their little faith, then rebukes the winds and the sea, and there is a great calm, so the men marvel and ask, “Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him?” (Matthew 8:27).

sections.title: Jesus Delivers Two Demon-Possessed Men
sections.summary: In the country of the Gergesenes two exceedingly fierce demon-possessed men meet Jesus, and the demons cry out, “What have we to do with You, Jesus, You Son of God?” (Matthew 8:29). At His word the demons go into a herd of swine, which runs into the sea and perishes, and the whole city comes out and begs Jesus to depart from their region.

1.brief: When Jesus comes down from the mountain, great crowds follow Him. The One who taught with authority on the mountain now displays that authority in His deeds.
1.explain:
“When He had come down from the mountain,”

Jesus had gone up on the mountain to teach His disciples (5:1), and the crowds listened in astonishment, “for He taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes” (7:28–29). Now He comes down. Matthew’s wording recalls Moses coming down from Mount Sinai with the word of God (Exodus 34:29). Moses, however, delivered a message he had received. Jesus spoke with His own authority: “But I say to you” (5:22, 28, 34, 39, 44).

Chapters 8 and 9 show that same authority in action. Matthew gathers ten miracles in these two chapters, revealing Jesus’ power over disease, demons, nature, sin, and death. The words of chapters 5–7 and the works of chapters 8–9 belong together, and Matthew frames both with nearly identical summaries of Jesus teaching, preaching, and healing (4:23; 9:35).

“great multitudes followed Him.”

The crowds that heard the Sermon on the Mount follow Jesus down the mountain. “Followed” becomes an important word in this chapter (8:10, 19, 22, 23). Some follow out of curiosity or need, one man offers to follow without counting the cost, and the disciples follow Jesus straight into a storm. Matthew lets the reader see that walking behind Jesus in a crowd is not yet the same as following Him as a disciple.
1.notes:
Matthew groups the miracles in three sets of three, with teaching on discipleship between the sets. The first set is the leper, the centurion’s servant, and Peter’s mother-in-law (8:1–15). The second is the storm, the two demon-possessed men, and the paralytic (8:23–9:8). The third is the ruler’s daughter together with the woman healed on the way, two blind men, and a mute man (9:18–34). The discipleship sections are 8:18–22 and 9:9–17. Counting the woman, there are ten miracles.

Matthew arranges this material by theme rather than strict sequence. Mark places the healing of Peter’s mother-in-law before the cleansing of the leper (Mark 1:29–45) and the calming of the storm much later (Mark 4:35–41). Both accounts are true to what happened. Matthew groups the events to display the breadth of Jesus’ authority.

2.brief: A leper comes, worships Jesus, and says, “Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.” He has no doubt about Jesus’ power; his only question is whether Jesus is willing.
2.explain:
“And behold, a leper came”

“Behold” calls attention to something startling. A leper approached Jesus in the middle of a crowd. Under the law of Moses, a person with leprosy was unclean. He had to tear his clothes, cover his mouth, cry out “Unclean! Unclean!” and live alone outside the camp (Leviticus 13:45–46). The disease damaged the body, but the uncleanness cut the person off from worship, from family life, and from ordinary human contact. For this man even to come near was a bold act.

“and worshiped Him,”

The man knelt or bowed low before Jesus. The Greek word can describe the honor given to any superior, but Matthew uses it again and again for people who come before Jesus in reverence (2:11; 14:33; 28:9, 17). Whatever this man fully understood, he approached Jesus as far more than an ordinary teacher or healer.

“saying, ‘Lord, if You are willing, You can make me clean.”

The man had no doubt about Jesus’ power: “You can.” His question was whether Jesus would want to help someone like him: “if You are willing.” He did not ask only to be healed but to be made “clean.” He wanted his disease removed and his place restored among God’s people.
2.notes:
The Hebrew term tsara’at in Leviticus 13–14 covers several skin conditions and is also applied to affected clothing and houses. It should not be equated in every occurrence with modern Hansen’s disease.

The Greek proskyneō refers to bowing down or prostrating oneself. The word occurs frequently in Matthew for people approaching Jesus.

3.brief: Jesus reaches out and touches him, saying, “I am willing; be cleansed,” and immediately the leprosy is gone. Jesus touches the untouchable, and instead of becoming unclean Himself, He makes the man clean.
3.explain:
“Then Jesus put out His hand and touched him,”

Jesus could have healed this man with a word, as He would heal the centurion’s servant (8:13). Instead, He reached out and touched him. Under the law, touching a leper made a person unclean (Leviticus 5:3), and people kept their distance. This man may not have felt a human hand in years. Jesus’ touch was deliberate. It met the man’s need for healing and his need to be received.

“saying, ‘I am willing; be cleansed.”

Jesus answers the man’s exact words. The man said, “If You are willing”; Jesus replies, “I am willing.” Then He speaks a command: “be cleansed.” He does not pray for the man or ask God to act. He speaks with His own authority, doing what Israel’s king had confessed only God could do (2 Kings 5:7).

“Immediately his leprosy was cleansed.”

The cleansing was immediate and complete. Normally, contact with a leper carried uncleanness to the one who touched him. Here the direction is reversed. Jesus was not made unclean by touching the leper; the leper was made clean by the touch of Jesus.
3.notes: Jesus’ reply is two words in Greek: thelō, katharisthēti (I will; be cleansed). The first echoes the leper’s own verb (“if You are willing”). Mark records that Jesus was “moved with compassion” before He touched him (Mark 1:41).

4.brief: Jesus tells the man to tell no one, but to show himself to the priest and offer the gift Moses commanded as a testimony to them. The healed man is to follow the law’s procedure, and his restoration will bear witness to the priests about what God is doing through Jesus.
4.explain:
“And Jesus said to him, ‘See that you tell no one;”

Jesus often limited publicity about His miracles (9:30; 12:16). Many people expected a Messiah who would win political freedom, and miracle stories spread quickly could stir crowds with the wrong expectations. Mark reports that this man did tell everyone, with the result that Jesus could no longer openly enter a town (Mark 1:45). The instruction also had an immediate purpose. Before the man told anyone else, he needed to go to the priest.

“but go your way, show yourself to the priest,”

The law required a person healed of leprosy to be examined by a priest, who alone could declare him clean and restore him to the community (Leviticus 14:1–3). Jesus had cleansed the man’s body, and He also cared about his restoration to worship, family, and community life.

“and offer the gift that Moses commanded,”

Leviticus 14 describes the offerings required of a cleansed leper. By sending the man to obey these instructions, Jesus honored the law of Moses. He had just said that He came not to destroy the Law but to fulfill it (5:17).

“as a testimony to them.”

“Them” most naturally refers to the priests, and through them to the people. A cleansed leper standing before the priest would be clear evidence that God was at work in Jesus. If the religious leaders received that evidence, it would confirm faith. If they refused Him, the same evidence would stand as a witness against their unbelief.
4.notes:
The priest went outside the camp to examine the healed person. One bird was killed over running water, and a living bird was dipped in its blood and released into the open field (Leviticus 14:3–7). After washing, shaving, and waiting seven days, the person brought guilt, sin, burnt, and grain offerings on the eighth day, and the priest applied blood and oil to the right ear, right thumb, and right big toe (Leviticus 14:8–20). The law made provision for those who could not afford the full offering (Leviticus 14:21–32).

The expression “a testimony to them” also occurs in Matthew 10:18; compare 24:14. The phrase can refer to evidence or witness presented to others.

5.brief: When Jesus enters Capernaum, a centurion comes to Him pleading for help. A Gentile officer of the occupying army comes to Israel’s King as a humble petitioner.
5.explain:
“Now when Jesus had entered Capernaum,”

Capernaum, on the northern shore of the Sea of Galilee, had become Jesus’ home base for His ministry (4:13). It was a fishing town on a trade route, with a customs office (9:9) and soldiers stationed to keep order.

“a centurion came to Him, pleading with Him,”

A centurion was a military officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers. Galilee was ruled by Herod Antipas, so this officer may have served in Herod’s forces, which were organized on the Roman pattern. Either way, he was a Gentile and a representative of foreign power. Luke adds that he loved the Jewish nation and had built their synagogue (Luke 7:5).

This man held real authority, yet he came to Jesus “pleading.” The verb describes earnest, urgent appeal. A man used to giving orders now stood before Jesus as a petitioner.
5.notes: Luke reports that the centurion sent Jewish elders and then friends to speak for him (Luke 7:3–6), while Matthew presents the centurion speaking directly. In the ancient world, a request made through representatives was counted as the act of the one who sent them. Matthew shortens the account and focuses on the centurion’s own words and faith. A similar compression appears when Matthew says the mother of James and John made a request that Mark attributes to the brothers themselves (20:20; Mark 10:35).

6.brief: The centurion says, “Lord, my servant is lying at home paralyzed, dreadfully tormented.” He brings Jesus the suffering of someone under his care.
6.explain:
“saying, ‘Lord, my servant is lying at home paralyzed,”

“Lord” can be a respectful “sir,” but the centurion’s words that follow show that he sees far more in Jesus than an ordinary man. The word for “servant” can mean either a servant or a child. Luke uses the ordinary word for a slave and adds that he was “dear to him” (Luke 7:2). The servant was “lying at home,” unable to move, and could not be brought to Jesus.

“dreadfully tormented.”

The servant’s condition was severe. “Tormented” describes intense suffering, and “dreadfully” makes it stronger. Luke reports that he was “ready to die” (Luke 7:2).

The centurion describes the need without making a specific request. He lays the situation before Jesus and trusts Him to respond.
6.notes:
Matthew’s word (pais) can mean “boy,” “child,” or “servant.” Luke’s use of doulos (“slave”) confirms that the sick man was a servant in the household (Luke 7:2, 10).

The verb basanizō originally described testing metals with a touchstone and came to mean torture or severe distress. The demons use the same word in 8:29: “Have You come here to torment us?” The servant suffered torment from his affliction; the demons fear torment from Jesus.

7.brief: Jesus answers, “I will come and heal him.” He responds readily to the request of this Gentile.
7.explain:
“And Jesus said to him, ‘I will come and heal him.”

Jesus responds without hesitation. He offers to go in person. Many devout Jews avoided entering a Gentile home because they considered it unclean (Acts 10:28; John 18:28). Jesus does not raise that concern. Just as He touched the leper, He is ready to go under a Gentile’s roof.

The “I” is emphatic in the Greek, as if Jesus said, I Myself will come. He promises both His presence and His healing.
7.notes: Some interpreters read Jesus’ words as a question: Shall I come and heal him? On that reading, Jesus would be testing the centurion’s faith in a way similar to His answer to the Canaanite woman (15:24–26). The Greek allows either reading. The NKJV and most translations render it as a statement, which fits Jesus’ immediate willingness in 8:3.

8.brief: The centurion replies that he is not worthy for Jesus to come under his roof, and asks Him only to speak a word so that his servant will be healed. He combines humility about himself with complete confidence in the power of Jesus’ word.
8.explain:
“The centurion answered and said, ‘Lord, I am not worthy that You should come under my roof.”

The centurion may have been aware of Jewish concerns about entering a Gentile home, and he may have wanted to spare Jesus any difficulty. But his words go deeper than custom. He recognized the greatness of the One standing before him and his own unworthiness to receive Him. Luke records that the Jewish elders said of him, “The one for whom He should do this was deserving” (Luke 7:4). The centurion did not see himself that way.

“But only speak a word, and my servant will be healed.”

The centurion believed that Jesus’ presence was not required for His power to work. A word from Jesus would be enough, whatever the distance. Scripture says of God, “He sent His word and healed them” (Psalm 107:20). The centurion attributes that kind of authority to the word of Jesus.
8.notes:
The adjective hikanos means sufficient or qualified. John uses the same adjective when saying he is not worthy to carry Jesus’ sandals (3:11).

Literally, only say with a word. The centurion’s confidence anticipates 8:16, where Jesus casts out spirits “with a word.”

9.brief: The centurion explains that he too is a man under authority, with soldiers who go and come at his command. He recognizes that Jesus holds authority over sickness the way an officer commands his soldiers, so a word from Him is enough.
9.explain:
“For I also am a man under authority,”

The word “also” is important. The centurion compares himself with Jesus. His own authority did not come from himself. He could command soldiers because he stood under the authority of his superiors and, ultimately, the emperor. He recognized that Jesus likewise acted under the authority of God, and that God’s authority stood behind Jesus’ commands.

“having soldiers under me. And I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it.”

In the army, orders are obeyed without the officer needing to be present at the place where they are carried out. The centurion reasoned that sickness would obey Jesus the same way his soldiers obeyed him. Jesus did not need to come to the house. He needed only to give the command.

10.brief: Jesus marvels and tells His followers that He has not found such great faith, “not even in Israel!” This outsider’s trust in Jesus’ authority surpasses what Jesus has found among His own people.
10.explain:
“When Jesus heard it, He marveled,”

The Gospels record only two occasions when Jesus marveled. Here He marvels at a Gentile’s faith. In Nazareth He marvels at His own townspeople’s unbelief (Mark 6:6). Jesus was genuinely moved by what He heard from this man.

“and said to those who followed,”

Jesus turns to the crowd that had followed Him from the mountain (8:1). The centurion’s faith becomes a lesson for those who were following Jesus.

“Assuredly, I say to you, I have not found such great faith, not even in Israel!”

“Assuredly” introduces a solemn statement. Israel had the Scriptures, the promises, the temple, and the prophets. Yet the greatest faith Jesus had yet encountered came from a Gentile soldier. The comparison does not deny that there was faith in Israel. Jesus’ own disciples were Jewish. It shows that faith, not privilege, is what receives from Jesus. The centurion’s faith was great because he trusted the authority of Jesus’ word without needing anything more.
10.notes:
The Greek is amēn, the Hebrew word for “truly” or so be it. People normally said “amen” to affirm what someone else had said. Jesus uniquely used it at the beginning of His own statements to underline their certainty and authority. Matthew records this usage more than thirty times.

Matthew contrasts the “great faith” of Gentiles (here and the Canaanite woman in 15:28) with the “little faith” of the disciples (8:26; 14:31; 16:8).

11.brief: Jesus declares that many will come from east and west to sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. The centurion’s faith anticipates people from all nations sharing in the feast of God’s promised kingdom.
11.explain:
“And I say to you that many will come from east and west,”

The prophets spoke of people being gathered to God “from the east” and “from the west” (Isaiah 43:5–6; 49:12; Psalm 107:3; Malachi 1:11). In several of these passages, scattered Israel is gathered home. In this setting, prompted by a Gentile’s faith, Jesus includes the nations among the “many.” God promised Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him (Genesis 12:3), and Matthew opens by calling Jesus “the Son of Abraham” (1:1).

“and sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob”

“Sit down” means to recline at a meal. Isaiah foresaw a great feast that the LORD would prepare “for all people” on His mountain (Isaiah 25:6–8). Gentiles who come by faith will share table fellowship with Israel’s patriarchs, the fathers of the promise.

“in the kingdom of heaven.”

The feast belongs to the kingdom in its full and final form. The kingdom Jesus announced (4:17) is already breaking in through His ministry, and it will be completed when He returns.
11.notes:
Guests at formal meals commonly reclined on couches around a low table, supported on the left elbow.

Some interpreters understand the “many” as Jews scattered among the nations. Others understand them as Gentiles, pointing to the centurion’s identity and the contrast with the “sons of the kingdom” in the next verse.

12.brief: But “the sons of the kingdom” will be cast into outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Those who presume on their heritage without trusting the King will be shut out, so inherited privilege cannot replace faith.
12.explain:
“But the sons of the kingdom”

“Sons of” is a Hebrew way of describing those who belong to something or seem to be its natural heirs. Here it refers to those within Israel who assumed the kingdom was theirs by birth and religious privilege. John the Baptist had warned against this kind of confidence: “Do not think to say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’” (3:9). Jesus is not condemning Israel as a people. Jesus Himself, His apostles, and the first believers were Jewish. The warning is directed at those who rely on heritage rather than faith.

“will be cast out into outer darkness.”

The feast of 8:11 is pictured as a brightly lit banquet hall. Outside is darkness. To be “cast out” is to be shut out of the kingdom’s celebration and fellowship. Jesus uses this same picture for final judgment in His later parables (22:13; 25:30).

“There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth.”

Weeping expresses grief and regret. Gnashing of teeth expresses anguish and bitter frustration. Here the warning falls on those who relied on inherited privilege. They assumed their place at the feast was secure, yet they will find themselves outside, grieving what they have lost while others from far away sit down with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Jesus speaks plainly and soberly so that no one will trust in heritage instead of faith in Him.
12.notes: In 13:38 the same phrase describes the good seed, the true people of the kingdom. The meaning depends on context. Here it describes those who appeared to be heirs; there it describes those who truly are.

13.brief: Jesus tells the centurion, “Go your way; and as you have believed, so let it be done for you,” and the servant is healed that very hour. Jesus’ word heals from a distance, just as the centurion trusted it would.
13.explain:
“Then Jesus said to the centurion, ‘Go your way;”

Jesus grants the request by sending the centurion home. He does not go to the house. The centurion asked for a word, and he receives one.

“and as you have believed, so let it be done for you.”

The centurion’s faith did not produce the healing. Jesus’ authority did. But faith received what Jesus gave. Jesus links the outcome to the centurion’s trust, as He will again with two blind men (9:29) and the Canaanite woman (15:28).

“And his servant was healed that same hour.”

The healing took place at the moment Jesus spoke, though Jesus was not present in the house. The timing confirms that the word of Jesus accomplished it. The centurion’s confidence in 8:8 was proven true.
13.notes: Matthew uses this kind of time note to show that healing came at Jesus’ word, not by gradual natural recovery (9:22; 15:28; 17:18). John records a similar healing at a distance for a royal official in Capernaum, where the father later confirmed that his son recovered at the very hour Jesus spoke (John 4:46–53). The two accounts describe different events.

14.brief: Entering Peter’s house, Jesus sees Peter’s mother-in-law lying sick with a fever. The King’s compassion reaches into the ordinary home of one of His disciples.
14.explain:
“Now when Jesus had come into Peter’s house,”

Peter’s house was in Capernaum (Mark 1:21, 29). Peter, also called Simon, was married, and his wife later traveled with him in ministry (1 Corinthians 9:5). The house appears to have served as a home base for Jesus while He ministered in Capernaum.

“He saw his wife’s mother lying sick with a fever.”

Matthew emphasizes that Jesus saw her. Mark and Luke mention that others told Jesus about her (Mark 1:30; Luke 4:38), but Matthew keeps the focus on Jesus’ own attention and initiative. Fevers in the ancient world could be dangerous and even fatal. Luke, the physician, describes it as a “high fever” (Luke 4:38). She was “lying” in bed, unable to carry out her normal responsibilities in the household.
14.notes:
Mark and Luke place this healing on a Sabbath, immediately after Jesus taught and cast out a demon in the Capernaum synagogue (Mark 1:21–31; Luke 4:31–39). Matthew omits the synagogue scene and places this healing as the third of his first set of three miracles.

Excavations in Capernaum have uncovered a first-century house beneath the remains of an octagonal fifth-century church. Early Christians appear to have venerated the house as Peter’s, and it was later converted into a place of worship. The identification cannot be proven, but it is supported by early tradition and the archaeological evidence.

15.brief: Jesus touches the hand of Peter’s mother-in-law, the fever leaves, and she rises and serves them. Her healing is complete and immediate, and she responds by serving Jesus.
15.explain:
“So He touched her hand,”

Once again Jesus heals through touch, as He did with the leper (8:3). Taking the hand of a sick woman in her own house was a personal and tender act. Jesus does not stand at a distance.

“and the fever left her.”

The fever departed immediately. Luke says Jesus “rebuked the fever” (Luke 4:39), using the same word Jesus uses when He rebukes the wind and sea (8:26). Sickness responds to Jesus’ authority.

“And she arose and served them.”

She did not need a period of recovery. A fever normally leaves a person weak, but she rose immediately and began to serve. Her strength was fully restored. Her serving also expressed gratitude. Having been touched by Jesus, she turned to care for Him and those with Him.
15.notes:
The NKJV follows the majority of Greek manuscripts, which read “served them.” Many older manuscripts read “served Him,” which keeps the focus on Jesus throughout the account. Mark and Luke both read “served them” (Mark 1:31; Luke 4:39).

The Greek diakoneō is the root of the word “deacon.” Matthew later uses it for the women who followed Jesus from Galilee and ministered to Him (27:55), and for Jesus Himself, who “did not come to be served, but to serve” (20:28).

16.brief: That evening people bring Jesus many who are demon-possessed, and He casts out the spirits with a word and heals all who are sick. Jesus has authority over both demonic powers and disease, and Matthew keeps the two distinct.
16.explain:
“When evening had come,”

Mark explains why the people waited until evening: it had been the Sabbath (Mark 1:21, 32). The Sabbath ended at sunset, and only then could people carry the sick through the town without breaking the Sabbath traditions. As soon as it was allowed, they came.

“they brought to Him many who were demon-possessed.”

“Demon-possessed” translates a word that describes people under the control or severe influence of evil spirits. Matthew distinguishes these people from those who were simply sick (see also 4:24; 10:8). The Gospels do not treat every illness as demonic, but they plainly present demonic oppression as real.

“And He cast out the spirits with a word,”

Jesus did not use rituals, objects, or long incantations. He simply spoke, and the spirits had to leave. This is the same authority the centurion recognized in Jesus’ word (8:8).

“and healed all who were sick,”

No one was turned away. Jesus healed every sick person brought to Him that evening. Matthew stresses the completeness of Jesus’ healing ministry (4:24; 12:15; 14:36).
16.notes:
The Greek daimonizomai means to be demonized, under the influence or control of a demon. Some prefer “demonized” because “possessed” can suggest ownership. The Gospels describe a range of effects, including violence, self-harm, muteness, blindness, and seizures (8:28; 9:32; 12:22; 17:15).

Josephus describes an exorcist using a ring with a root and reciting Solomon’s name (Antiquities 8.46–49). Such reports illustrate exorcistic practices involving objects and spoken formulas.

17.brief: Jesus’ healings fulfill Isaiah’s words, “He Himself took our infirmities And bore our sicknesses.” They show the Servant already lifting the burdens of the people, and they belong to the full redemption He secures, whose complete bodily restoration awaits the resurrection.
17.explain:
“that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah the prophet, saying:”

Matthew often shows how Jesus fulfills the Old Testament Scriptures (1:22; 2:15; 4:14). Here he quotes Isaiah 53, the great prophecy of the Suffering Servant who would bear the sins of many and be wounded for their transgressions (Isaiah 53:5–6, 12).

“He Himself took our infirmities”

The word translated “infirmities” refers to weakness and illness. “He Himself” emphasizes that Jesus personally took them up. He did not only sympathize with the sick; He took their weaknesses away from them.

“And bore our sicknesses.”

“Bore” means to carry a burden. Isaiah’s prophecy describes the Servant carrying what belonged to others. Matthew translates Isaiah’s Hebrew directly and highlights its physical meaning: sickness and pain.

Isaiah 53 describes the Servant’s sufferings for His people, culminating in His death. By applying this verse to Jesus’ healing ministry, Matthew shows that Jesus’ healings flow from the same redemptive mission that would take Him to the cross. The One who would bear our sins also bears our sicknesses. Healing is part of what Jesus came to accomplish for His people, not something separate from His saving work. What Christians experience now as healing is a foretaste of what will be complete at the resurrection, when the body is fully redeemed (Romans 8:23). Believers can pray for healing with bold expectation, and the Spirit still gives gifts of healings as He wills (1 Corinthians 12:9–11). Persistent illness is never a basis for condemning a sufferer’s faith or character.
17.notes: In Isaiah 53:4 the Hebrew words (choli and mak’ov) literally mean “sicknesses” and “pains.” The NKJV of Isaiah renders them “griefs” and “sorrows.” The Septuagint translated the verse as he bears our sins, giving it a spiritual meaning. Matthew does not follow the Septuagint here. He renders the Hebrew directly and keeps its emphasis on physical affliction.

18.brief: Seeing great crowds around Him, Jesus gives the command to cross to the other side of the sea. His movement away from the crowd sets the stage for testing who will truly follow Him.
18.explain:
“And when Jesus saw great multitudes about Him,”

The healings in Capernaum drew even larger crowds. Jesus’ response was not to stay where His popularity was growing.

“He gave a command to depart to the other side.”

“The other side” means the eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee, a largely Gentile region. Jesus’ command moves the story toward the storm (8:23–27) and the deliverance of the demon-possessed men (8:28–34). Before the boat leaves, two men come to Jesus about following Him, and their conversations raise the question of what it means to go where He goes.
18.notes:
The lake is about thirteen miles long and eight miles wide, lying roughly seven hundred feet below sea level and surrounded by hills. Its eastern shore belonged mostly to the Decapolis, a league of Greek-speaking cities with a largely Gentile population.

Luke records these two exchanges, along with a third, as Jesus begins His journey to Jerusalem (Luke 9:57–62). Matthew places them before the crossing, so that the call to follow Jesus is immediately tested in the storm.

19.brief: A scribe comes and says, “Teacher, I will follow You wherever You go.” His offer sounds wholehearted, but he may not yet understand what following Jesus involves.
19.explain:
“Then a certain scribe came and said to Him,”

Scribes were experts in the law of Moses who taught, interpreted, and copied the Scriptures. In Matthew they usually appear as opponents of Jesus, and the crowds had just contrasted Jesus’ teaching with theirs (7:29). This scribe, however, was drawn to Jesus.

“Teacher, I will follow You wherever You go.”

The scribe calls Jesus “Teacher,” a title of respect. His promise sounds wholehearted: “wherever You go.” In Jewish practice, a student would choose a rabbi and attach himself to that teacher. The scribe offers himself on his own initiative, with the confidence of someone who has not yet considered where Jesus is going.
19.notes:
In Matthew, the disciples address Jesus as “Lord,” while outsiders and opponents usually call Him “Teacher” (9:11; 12:38; 19:16; 22:16, 24, 36). Judas is the exception among the Twelve, calling Jesus “Rabbi” (26:25, 49). The scribe’s address may suggest that he saw Jesus as a great teacher but not yet as Lord.

Disciples of rabbis usually chose their teacher. Jesus reversed this pattern by calling His disciples Himself (4:19, 21; 9:9; John 15:16).

20.brief: Jesus answers that foxes have holes and birds have nests, “but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.” Following Jesus means sharing His life without settled security or comfort.
20.explain:
“And Jesus said to him, ‘Foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests,”

Even wild animals have a place to rest and shelter. Foxes have their dens, and birds have their nests.

“but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head.”

This is the first time Matthew records Jesus calling Himself “the Son of Man.” It was His favorite way of referring to Himself. The title points back to Daniel’s vision of “One like the Son of Man” who comes with the clouds of heaven and receives everlasting dominion over all peoples (Daniel 7:13–14). The One who will rule every nation had no settled home during His earthly ministry.

Jesus was not saying that He never slept indoors. He had just been in Peter’s house. He meant that His mission kept Him moving, with no home of His own and no guaranteed welcome. At the end of this chapter, a whole region will ask Him to leave (8:34). Anyone who follows Jesus must be willing to share that same uncertainty and rejection.
20.notes: “Son of Man” occurs about thirty times in Matthew, almost always in Jesus’ speech. The corresponding Hebrew expression can mean a human being, as in Psalm 8:4 and Ezekiel 2:1.

21.brief: Another disciple says, “Lord, let me first go and bury my father.” He asks to put a family duty ahead of following Jesus now.
21.explain:
“Then another of His disciples said to Him,”

This man is already counted among Jesus’ disciples in a broader sense. The scribe offered too quickly; this man hesitates.

“Lord, let me first go and bury my father.”

He calls Jesus “Lord,” but his request places something else “first.” Burying one’s father was among the most sacred duties in Jewish life, connected to the command to honor father and mother (Exodus 20:12). Jewish tradition considered it so important that it released a son from other religious obligations.

It is unlikely that the man’s father had just died. Burial normally took place on the day of death, and a grieving son would have been at home with the family, not standing among the crowd with Jesus. The man was most likely asking to remain at home until his father died and was buried, which might be months or years away. Either way, he wanted to follow Jesus later, after fulfilling his family obligations.
21.notes:
Jewish burial usually took place within a day of death. In some cases, the bones were gathered about a year later and placed in a stone box called an ossuary, a practice known as secondary burial. Some interpreters suggest the man was asking to wait until this second burial. Both possibilities involve an indefinite delay.

The Mishnah exempts a man whose dead relative lies before him from reciting the daily Shema and other prayers until the burial is complete (Berakhot 3:1). This shows how seriously burial obligations were taken.

22.brief: Jesus answers, “Follow Me, and let the dead bury their own dead.” With startling urgency He insists that following Him cannot be put on hold, and others who are spiritually dead can tend to such duties.
22.explain:
“But Jesus said to him, ‘Follow Me,”

Jesus repeats the call He gave His first disciples (4:19). The tense of the Greek suggests continuing action: keep following Me, now.

“and let the dead bury their own dead.”

This is a striking statement. Jesus uses the word “dead” in two senses. Those who are spiritually dead, who have not responded to the kingdom, can take care of burying the physically dead. The man’s calling was to follow the One who brings life. Luke adds Jesus’ words, “but you go and preach the kingdom of God” (Luke 9:60).

Jesus was not teaching disrespect for parents. He rebuked the Pharisees for using religious excuses to avoid caring for their parents (15:3–6). His point was that no obligation, however sacred, may come before Him. Only God could rightly make such a claim, and Jesus makes it as His own.

23.brief: Jesus gets into a boat, and His disciples follow Him. Those who have answered His call now go where He goes, into the storm that follows.
23.explain:
“Now when He got into a boat,”

Jesus carries out the command He gave in 8:18 to cross to the other side. The boat was likely a fishing boat, the kind several of the disciples had worked from before Jesus called them (4:18–22).

“His disciples followed Him.”

Matthew uses the same word that has just been at the center of Jesus’ conversations about discipleship (8:19, 22). Having heard what it costs to follow Jesus, the disciples now follow Him literally, into a boat and onto the sea. Their following will lead them straight into a storm.
23.notes:
In 1986, during a drought, the remains of a first-century fishing boat were discovered in the mud on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee. It is about 27 feet long and 7.5 feet wide and could have carried around a dozen people. It gives a good picture of the kind of boat Jesus and His disciples used.

Mark places the storm on the evening after Jesus taught in parables by the sea, and notes that the disciples took Him along in the boat just as He was (Mark 4:35–36). Matthew connects the event to the teaching on following Jesus.

24.brief: Suddenly a great storm arises on the sea, so violent that the waves cover the boat, but Jesus is asleep. His calm rest stands in sharp contrast to the danger around Him.
24.explain:
“And suddenly a great tempest arose on the sea,”

The Sea of Galilee is known for sudden, violent storms. Cool air can rush down through the surrounding hills and ravines onto the warm water below and whip the lake into dangerous waves with little warning. Matthew’s word for “tempest” is the word usually translated “earthquake” (24:7; 27:54; 28:2). It describes a violent shaking, and this was a “great” one.

“so that the boat was covered with the waves.”

The waves were breaking over the boat, threatening to swamp it. The disciples included experienced fishermen who knew these waters, and they believed they were about to die (8:25).

“But He was asleep.”

In the middle of the danger, Jesus was sleeping. His sleep reveals His true humanity. After the long days of teaching and healing in Capernaum, He was exhausted. His sleep also reveals His complete trust in His Father. The psalmist wrote, “I will both lie down in peace, and sleep; for You alone, O LORD, make me dwell in safety” (Psalm 4:8).

The scene recalls Jonah, who slept in a ship during a great storm (Jonah 1:4–6). But Jonah slept while running from God. Jesus slept in perfect obedience to Him.
24.notes: The Greek seismos is the source of the English word “seismic.” Matthew uses it for the earthquakes at Jesus’ death and resurrection (27:54; 28:2) and among the signs of the end (24:7). Mark and Luke use a different word for a windstorm (Mark 4:37; Luke 8:23).

25.brief: The disciples wake Jesus, crying, “Lord, save us! We are perishing!” In their terror they turn to the only One who can help.
25.explain:
“Then His disciples came to Him and awoke Him,”

In their fear, the disciples turned to Jesus. Whatever their fear, they knew where to go.

“saying, ‘Lord, save us! We are perishing!”

Their words are a short, urgent prayer. They call Him “Lord” and ask Him to “save.” Their cry expresses both faith and fear. They believe Jesus can help, but they are convinced they are about to die. “We are perishing” expresses their panic; they believed death was moments away.

The word “save” connects to Jesus’ name. The angel told Joseph, “You shall call His name JESUS, for He will save His people from their sins” (1:21). The disciples cry out to the Savior to save them from death.
25.notes: Mark records “Teacher, do You not care that we are perishing?” (Mark 4:38); Luke has “Master, Master, we are perishing!” (Luke 8:24). Matthew records “Lord, save us! We are perishing!”

26.brief: Jesus asks why they are afraid, calling them “O you of little faith,” then rises and rebukes the winds and the sea, and there is a great calm. He addresses their fear first, then commands creation itself, and the storm obeys Him completely.
26.explain:
“But He said to them, ‘Why are you fearful, O you of little faith?”

In Matthew, Jesus speaks to the disciples before He speaks to the storm. The question is not harsh condemnation but a loving rebuke. They had seen Jesus heal lepers, cast out demons, and heal at a distance. Jesus Himself was in the boat with them. Their fear showed that their faith had not yet grown to match what they had seen.

“Little faith” is not the same as no faith. They did cry out to Jesus. But their faith was too small to hold steady under pressure. Matthew uses this word for the disciples several times (6:30; 14:31; 16:8).

“Then He arose and rebuked the winds and the sea,”

Jesus stood and spoke to the wind and the waves. “Rebuked” is the same word Jesus uses when He rebukes demons (17:18). He commanded creation as its Master. In the Old Testament, it is the LORD who rebukes the sea (Psalm 104:7; 106:9; Nahum 1:4).

“and there was a great calm.”

The “great tempest” of 8:24 is matched by a “great calm.” Normally, waves continue rolling long after the wind dies down. Here the sea became calm immediately.
26.notes:
The Greek oligopistos appears almost only in Matthew (6:30; 8:26; 14:31; 16:8); the one other use is Luke 12:28. Many manuscripts also read the related noun “little faith” in 17:20, where the NKJV, following the majority of manuscripts, reads “unbelief.” The word describes genuine but weak faith.

The verb epitimaō, “rebuke,” is also used of addressing demons and, in Luke 4:39, a fever. Mark 4:39 records the command “Peace, be still!”

In Mark and Luke, Jesus calms the storm first and then addresses the disciples’ faith (Mark 4:39–40; Luke 8:24–25). Matthew places His question first, emphasizing the disciples’ faith.

27.brief: The men marvel, asking, “Who can this be, that even the winds and the sea obey Him?” Jesus’ command over the sea raises the question of His identity, since such authority belongs to God.
27.explain:
“So the men marveled,”

The disciples’ fear of the storm turned into awe of Jesus. Matthew calls them “the men,” which may draw a contrast between ordinary human beings and the One who commands creation.

“saying, ‘Who can this be,”

This is the right question, and it runs through Matthew’s Gospel. The disciples’ understanding grows until Peter declares, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (16:16). In the Old Testament, only God stills the sea: “You rule the raging of the sea; when its waves rise, You still them” (Psalm 89:9; see also Psalm 65:7; 107:29; Job 38:8–11).

“that even the winds and the sea obey Him?”

The word “even” is important. The disciples had seen sickness and demons obey Jesus. Now creation itself obeys Him. The centurion had compared Jesus’ word to an officer’s command that is obeyed (8:9). Here the winds and waves obey His command.

28.brief: On the other side, in the country of the Gergesenes, two demon-possessed men come out of the tombs to meet Him, so fierce that no one can pass that way. Jesus enters territory ruled by fear and darkness.
28.explain:
“When He had come to the other side, to the country of the Gergesenes,”

Jesus and the disciples arrived on the eastern shore, the destination He commanded in 8:18. This was largely Gentile territory, part of the region of the Decapolis. The herd of pigs in 8:30 fits this predominantly Gentile setting, though it does not tell us the identity of everyone who lived there. Matthew’s focus, like that of the parallel accounts, is on the men Jesus delivered (Mark 5:1–2; Luke 8:26–27).

“there met Him two demon-possessed men,”

Mark and Luke focus on one man, probably the more prominent of the two and the one who spoke (Mark 5:2; Luke 8:27). Matthew mentions both. Mentioning one does not deny that there were two.

“coming out of the tombs,”

Tombs were often caves or chambers cut into hillsides. To Jews, they were places of ritual uncleanness (Numbers 19:16). These men lived among the dead, separated from normal life. Isaiah describes rebellious people who “sit among the graves” and “eat swine’s flesh” (Isaiah 65:4), and this scene shows that kind of defilement.

“exceedingly fierce, so that no one could pass that way.”

The men were violent and dangerous. Mark adds that no one could bind the man even with chains, and that he cried out day and night and cut himself with stones (Mark 5:3–5). The demonic power controlling them had made a whole road impassable. People avoided the area entirely.
28.notes:
The manuscripts vary in all three Gospels. The NKJV follows the majority of manuscripts in reading “Gergesenes” here, while many older manuscripts read “Gadarenes” in Matthew and “Gerasenes” in Mark and Luke. Gadara was a major city about six miles southeast of the lake, and its territory may have extended to the shore. Gerasa was a city more than thirty miles away. Gergesa is often identified with the site of Kursi on the eastern shore, where a steep slope comes near the water. The differences most likely reflect different ways of naming the same general area, by a nearby village, a regional city, or the wider district.

Matthew records two men, while Mark 5:2 and Luke 8:27 concentrate on one. A similar difference occurs in the accounts of the blind men near Jericho (Matthew 20:30; Mark 10:46; Luke 18:35).

29.brief: The demons cry out, “What have we to do with You, Jesus, You Son of God?” and ask whether He has come to torment them “before the time.” They recognize who He is and know that their appointed judgment is coming.
29.explain:
“And suddenly they cried out, saying,”

The demons spoke through the men. The sudden cry shows that they recognized Jesus as soon as He arrived.

“What have we to do with You, Jesus, You Son of God?”

“What have we to do with You?” is an expression of hostility and self-defense, meaning, What do we have in common? or “Why are you interfering with us?” (compare 1 Kings 17:18). The demons immediately identify Jesus as “the Son of God.” The disciples had just asked, “Who can this be?” (8:27), and the demons know the answer at once. Their knowledge did not produce faith or submission. James writes that the demons believe that God is one, “and tremble” (James 2:19).

“Have You come here to torment us before the time?”

The demons knew that a time of final judgment had been appointed for them (25:41; Revelation 20:10). They feared that Jesus had come to carry out that judgment early. Their words reveal that their defeat is certain and their time is limited. The arrival of the King had already begun to break the enemy’s hold, ahead of the final judgment. Jesus would later say, “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, surely the kingdom of God has come upon you” (12:28).
29.notes:
The phrase translates a Hebrew idiom (literally, What to me and to you?). Its meaning depends on context, ranging from mild disagreement to strong hostility (Judges 11:12; 2 Samuel 16:10; John 2:4). Here it is clearly hostile.

This is the same verb used of the servant’s suffering in 8:6. The demons who tormented their victims now fear torment themselves.

30.brief: Some distance away a large herd of swine is feeding. The detail sets the scene in a largely Gentile region east of the Sea of Galilee.
30.explain:
“Now a good way off from them”

The herd was some distance from where Jesus met the men, but still within sight.

“there was a herd of many swine feeding.”

Pigs were unclean animals under the law of Moses, forbidden for Israel to eat (Leviticus 11:7; Deuteronomy 14:8). A large herd of pigs confirms that this was a Gentile area. Mark says there were about two thousand (Mark 5:13). This was a substantial investment for the owners and the local economy.
30.notes: Pig farming was practiced in Gentile communities of the region. Pigs were used for food and in some pagan sacrifices.

31.brief: The demons beg Jesus that if He casts them out, He will let them go into the herd of swine. Even the demons must ask His permission, showing they are entirely under His authority.
31.explain:
“So the demons begged Him, saying,”

The demons begged. The same word described the centurion pleading with Jesus (8:5). These powers that had terrorized a whole region now had to plead with Jesus.

“If You cast us out,”

The demons did not question whether Jesus could expel them. They assumed He would. Their only question was where they would go.

“permit us to go away into the herd of swine.”

The demons asked permission. They could not act without it. Spirits seek a place to dwell (12:43–45), and these demons wanted a body to inhabit rather than be sent away entirely. Luke records that they begged Jesus not to command them to go into the abyss (Luke 8:31).

32.brief: Jesus says, “Go,” and the demons go into the swine, and the whole herd rushes down the steep slope into the sea and dies. A single word from Jesus frees the men, and the herd’s destruction gives visible proof of the spirits’ departure and their destructive nature.
32.explain:
“And He said to them, ‘Go.”

One word was enough. Jesus did not argue or struggle. Earlier, He cast out spirits “with a word” (8:16); here the word is a single command.

“So when they had come out, they went into the herd of swine.”

The men were set free. The demons left them and entered the pigs, as they had asked.

“And suddenly the whole herd of swine ran violently down the steep place into the sea, and perished in the water.”

The result revealed the nature of the demons. They destroyed what they inhabited. What they did to the pigs in a moment, they had been doing to the men for years. The stampede also gave visible proof that the men had truly been delivered and showed the strength of the forces that had controlled them.

Scripture does not explain fully why Jesus permitted this. What it does make clear is that two human lives were worth more to Jesus than a herd of animals (12:12), and that the demons’ destructive nature was openly exposed.
32.notes: The command hupagete comes from the same verb used in Jesus’ instructions to the leper in 8:4 and the centurion in 8:13.

33.brief: Those tending the swine run to the city and report everything, including what happened to the demon-possessed men. News of the deliverance spreads through the region.
33.explain:
“Then those who kept them fled;”

The herdsmen had watched their entire herd rush into the sea. Frightened and responsible for the loss, they ran.

“and they went away into the city and told everything,”

They reported what had happened in the town. Their first concern was the herd.

“including what had happened to the demon-possessed men.”

Matthew’s wording places the men last, as if they were an addition to the main report. For the herdsmen, the main story was the loss of the pigs. The deliverance of two human beings came after.
33.notes: Mark 5:15 and Luke 8:35 describe the delivered man sitting, clothed, and in his right mind. Mark 5:18–20 records that Jesus sent him home to report what had happened.

34.brief: After hearing the herdsmen’s report, the whole city comes out to meet Jesus, and when they see Him, they beg Him to leave their region. The very One who has just set the two men free is asked to go away.
34.explain:
“And behold, the whole city came out to meet Jesus.”

“Behold” marks a surprising turn. The entire town came out to Jesus. The word for “meet” often describes a group going out formally to receive an important visitor. The reader might expect a welcome.

“And when they saw Him, they begged Him to depart from their region.”

Instead, they begged Jesus to leave. Luke explains that they were seized with great fear (Luke 8:37). They had seen power they could not control, and they had suffered a costly loss. Rather than receive the One who had set two of their own free, they wanted Him gone.

The chapter that opened with a leper asking to be made clean ends with a city begging Jesus to depart. Jesus respected their request. In the next verse, He gets into a boat and leaves (9:1).
34.notes:
The noun hupantēsis can refer to going out to meet someone, including a visiting official. A related word occurs in Matthew 25:1.

The word parakaleō (“beg,” “plead”) links three requests in this chapter: the centurion asks Jesus to heal (8:5), the demons ask Jesus to let them enter the swine (8:31), and the town asks Jesus to leave (8:34). Jesus grants all three.
